items.title: The posterior mean is the unique squared-loss Bayes action in a Hilbert target

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §5.3.1, PDF pp. 104–105
references.locator: Example 5.4 gives scalar posterior risk under squared error as a quadratic in the action and identifies its posterior-mean minimizer when expectations exist; the local proof extends the argument coordinatewise to a Hilbert target.

references.title: Giannis Daras et al., A Survey on Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems, arXiv:2410.00083v1
references.locator: Lemma A.1, PDF p. 25, proves a finite-dimensional conditional-mean/MMSE identity by expanding the square and conditioning the residual; it is supporting context only, while the Hilbert-target result is proved locally.

references.title: Masoumeh Dashti and Andrew M. Stuart, The Bayesian Approach to Inverse Problems, arXiv:1302.6989v4
references.locator: §3.2, Theorem 3.4 and proof, for an inverse posterior as a data-indexed conditional law; §4.1, Theorem 4.3 and proof, for posterior propriety and data-version hypotheses. Context only: the Hilbert-risk proof assumes a probability kernel directly and does not import this source proof.

items.axiom_use: Assume AC. It is used by the scalar L2 projection supplier; it also supplies the Countable Choice hypothesis of Parseval. The basis is supplied as part of the statement, and the remaining coordinate, kernel, and summation arguments require no additional choice axiom.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space, let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and fix a complete orthonormal basis $(e_j)_{j\in J}$, where $J$ is either finite with its supplied ordering or $J=\mathbb N$. A complex Hilbert signal space is included by viewing it as a real Hilbert space with inner product the real part of its complex inner product and supplying a real orthonormal basis. Let $\Pi$ be a probability kernel from $\mathsf Y$ to $H$ with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. Define
$$D_2:=\left\{y\in\mathsf Y:\int_H\|h\|_H^2\,\Pi_y(dh)<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $y\in D_2$ and $j\in J$, define
$$m_j(y):=\int_H\langle h,e_j\rangle_H\,\Pi_y(dh),\qquad \mu(y):=\sum_{j\in J}m_j(y)e_j,$$
where the last sum is the norm limit of its finite partial sums. Then $D_2\in\mathcal Y$, the sum defining $\mu(y)$ exists for every $y\in D_2$, and $\mu:D_2\to H$ is measurable. For every $y\in D_2$ and every action $a\in H$,
$$\int_H\|h-a\|_H^2\,\Pi_y(dh)=\int_H\|h-\mu(y)\|_H^2\,\Pi_y(dh)+\|a-\mu(y)\|_H^2.$$
Thus $\mu(y)$ is the unique finite-risk action minimizing posterior squared-error risk over all of $H$, and it is a measurable Bayes action rule on $D_2$. The minimization is over the full Hilbert space: the mean need not belong to a nonconvex admissible signal subset, and no perceptual-representativeness claim is made. For a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, let $Y:\Omega\to(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ and $T:\Omega\to H$ be measurable random elements with $E\|T\|_H^2<\infty$. If the same $\Pi$ is a supplied regular conditional law of $T$ given $Y$, write $P_Y(B)=P(Y\in B)$ for the law of $Y$. Then $D_2$ has full $P_Y$-measure. Extend $\mu$ by zero to a measurable map $\bar\mu:\mathsf Y\to H$; the coordinates of $\bar\mu(Y)$ are versions of $E[\langle T,e_j\rangle_H\mid\sigma(Y)]$, and $\bar\mu(Y)$ is square-integrable. Any square-integrable $H$-valued random variable whose basis coordinates are versions of those same conditional expectations equals $\bar\mu(Y)$ almost surely. The RCD's values on $P_Y$-null data sets remain version choices.

items.title: Learned inverse estimators and reconstruction targets

references.title: Gregory Ongie, Ajil Jalal, Christopher A. Metzler, Richard G. Baraniuk, Alexandros G. Dimakis, and Rebecca Willett, Deep Learning Techniques for Inverse Problems in Imaging, arXiv:2005.06001v1
references.locator: §3.1 and §4.1, PDF pp. 6–11, for matched training pairs, direct reconstruction maps, and finite unrolled updates; §4.2.1, PDF pp. 11–13, for denoisers and learned generative priors.

references.title: Giannis Daras et al., A Survey on Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems, arXiv:2410.00083v1
references.locator: §1.2 and §§2.4.2–2.4.3, PDF pp. 3 and 7–8, distinguish point reconstruction, score fields, conditional-score updates, and posterior sampling. The survey reports method-specific scope and does not establish generic sampler correctness.

references.title: Masoumeh Dashti and Andrew M. Stuart, The Bayesian Approach to Inverse Problems, arXiv:1302.6989v4
references.locator: §3.2, Theorem 3.4 and proof, for a supplied data-indexed posterior kernel and its evidence/version conventions; §4.1, Theorem 4.3, for posterior well-posedness under stated potential hypotheses.

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is required; all fitting laws, maps, and probability kernels are supplied as inputs.
items.statement:
Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric parameter and data spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth class, let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map, and let $(Q,d_Q)$ be a metric target space with a measurable target map $q:U\to Q$. The target $q(x)$ is the recovery object assigned to truth $x$; $Q$ may be the parameter space itself or a quotient solution-class space. All metric spaces in this definition carry their Borel sigma-algebras. A **point reconstruction rule** is a Borel map $g:Y\to Q$, and its output at data $y$ is $g(y)$. A **learned point estimator** is such a map $\widehat q_\phi$ with a fitted parameter $\phi$ in a specified parameter set. A complete training description names the probability law $P_{\rm fit}$ of all variables used to fit $\phi$; those variables may be paired or unpaired. A complete test description names a probability law $P_{\rm test}$ for evaluation pairs $(Y,q(X))$. No equality between fitting and test laws is assumed.

A finite **unrolled learned update** consists of an integer $K\geq1$, a Borel initialization $u_0:Y\to Q$, and Borel maps $T_{\phi,k}:Q\times Y\to Q$ for $0\leq k<K$, with $u_{k+1}(y)=T_{\phi,k}(u_k(y),y)$. Its output $u_K(y)$ is a point reconstruction rule. An **amortized inverse map** is a learned point estimator applied to multiple data inputs after a single fit; this term adds a reuse convention, not an accuracy guarantee.

For a real Hilbert signal space $H$, a **denoiser** is a Borel map $D_\phi:H\to H$ trained under a specified signal-corruption law and used to transform a corrupted signal into a signal estimate or an update. A denoiser is the exact minimum mean-square error map only when it equals the conditional mean for the specified signal and corruption laws. A **learned prior** is a supplied Borel probability measure $\rho_\phi$ on $H$; one construction is the pushforward law $\rho_\phi(A)=\nu(G_\phi^{-1}(A))$ of a specified probability $\nu$ under a Borel generator $G_\phi:Z\to H$. The law or generator alone is not a data-to-target estimator.

In a finite-dimensional signal space $\mathbb R^d$, a **score field model** is a Borel map $s_\phi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ intended to approximate $\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ for a specified family of positive continuously differentiable densities $p_t$. A score field is not itself a posterior law, posterior sample, or point reconstruction rule. A **posterior sampler** is a probability kernel $S:Y\to Q$; relative to a supplied posterior target kernel $\Pi_y$, it is exact on a data domain $D$ when $S_y=\Pi_y$ as probability measures for every $y\in D$. A draw from $S_y$ is random; obtaining a point estimate from it requires an additional summary rule. The name “learned” by itself asserts no exact recovery, stability, convergence, calibration, or train-to-test guarantee.

items.title: Inverse reconstruction risk under train and test laws

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §5.3.1, PDF pp. 104–105
references.locator: Definition 5.3 and Example 5.4: Bayes risk is average risk under a law, posterior risk is a conditional-data integral, and scalar squared-error posterior risk is minimized by the posterior mean when the expectations exist.

references.title: Peter Hoff, Statistical Decision Problems, §§4.1–4.2, PDF pp. 7–8
references.locator: The decision problem specifies the parameter, action space, loss, measurable decision rule and its risk as expected loss under the observation law.

references.title: Hongkai Zheng et al., InverseBench: Benchmarking Plug-and-Play Diffusion Priors for Inverse Problems in Physical Sciences, ICLR 2025
references.locator: §5 and Appendix C, PDF pp. 10 and 28–29, report selected empirical behavior under out-of-distribution sources and prior mismatch; these experiments imply no universal risk bound.

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is required; the joint evaluation laws and randomized kernels are supplied as inputs.
items.statement:
Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ and $(Q,\mathcal Q)$ be measurable data and target spaces, with $\mathcal Q$ the Borel sigma-algebra of the target metric space. Let $P$ be a probability measure on the product space $(\mathsf Y\times Q,\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal Q)$, and let $\ell:Q\times Q\to[0,+\infty]$ be product-measurable, where $\ell(t,a)$ is the loss for target $t$ and action $a$. For a Borel point reconstruction rule $g:\mathsf Y\to Q$, its risk under $P$ is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(g):=\int_{\mathsf Y\times Q}\ell(t,g(y))\,P(dy,dt).$$
For a randomized reconstruction rule given by a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathsf Y$ to $Q$, define
$$R_P(K):=\int_{\mathsf Y\times Q}\!\left(\int_Q\ell(t,a)\,K(y,da)\right)P(dy,dt).$$
The inner integral is measurable in $(y,t)$ by kernel integration; a deterministic rule is the special case $K_y=\delta_{g(y)}$. When $P_{\rm train}$ and $P_{\rm test}$ are specified joint laws on the same input-target space, the corresponding training-law risk and test-law risk are $R_{P_{\rm train}}(K)$ and $R_{P_{\rm test}}(K)$. Either value may be $+\infty$. This definition imposes no inequality between the two risks: any such comparison requires an additional assumption relating the joint laws or the rule's behavior under them.

title: Learned reconstruction targets and risk — Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A posterior mean can lie outside a nonconvex signal class
items.axiom_use: AC is inherited only through the general posterior-mean proposition; the finite posterior and risk calculations are choice-free.
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let the admissible signal set be $S=\{-1,1\}\subset\mathbb R$, which is nonconvex because it omits the midpoint $0$, let the target be the signal itself, and let the data space consist of one point $Y=\{0\}$. Use the constant forward map $F(t)=0$ and the prior assigning probability $1/2$ to each signal. The posterior law at the sole datum is therefore $\Pi_0=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_1$. Under squared loss on the full action space $\mathbb R$, the posterior mean is $0$, which is outside $S$; its posterior risk at action $a$ is $1+a^2$, so its unique unconstrained minimum is $1$ at $a=0$. If actions are restricted to $S$, both admissible actions have risk $2$. The proposition concerns the full Hilbert action space and does not assert that the posterior mean is an admissible signal.

items.title: A train/test prior shift changes reconstruction risk
items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the two laws and the deterministic forward map are explicit finite objects.
items.statement: Let the truth space and target space both be $U=Q=\{0,1\}\subset\mathbb R$, let the target map be the identity, let the data space be $Y=\{0\}$, and let the deterministic forward map be $F(t)=0$ for both truths. Use squared loss $\ell(t,a)=(t-a)^2$ and the point reconstruction rule $g(0)=0$. Let the training prior be $\pi_{\rm train}=\delta_0$ and the test prior be $\pi_{\rm test}=\delta_1$. The resulting joint laws of data and target are $P_{\rm train}=\delta_{(0,0)}$ and $P_{\rm test}=\delta_{(0,1)}$. The input marginal is the same in both laws, but $R_{P_{\rm train}}(g)=0$ and $R_{P_{\rm test}}(g)=1$; equality of input marginals alone does not bound target-risk change under prior shift.

items.title: An exact posterior sample need not minimize point risk
items.axiom_use: AC is inherited only through the general posterior-mean proposition; the finite probability law and calculations are choice-free.
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ take values $-1$ and $1$ with equal probabilities, let $Y=0$ deterministically, and use the squared-error loss on $\mathbb R$. The posterior is $\Pi_0=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_1$. Given $Y=0$, draw $\widetilde T$ independently of $T$ from $\Pi_0$. Here **exact posterior calibration** means $\mathcal L(\widetilde T\mid Y=0)=\Pi_0$, which holds because the sampler kernel is $S_0=\Pi_0$. The posterior mean action $0$ has posterior risk $1$, while the expected squared error between the true posterior draw and the independent posterior sample is $2$. Thus even an exactly calibrated posterior sample is not the Bayes-optimal point action and is not itself the posterior mean.
